name: Rafael Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior marketing executive at a coffee roaster. We sell bags of coffee in supermarkets and supply about forty cafés. I write the back-of-bag text, the café menu boards and the seasonal promotions, like the autumn blend, and I chase the printers when the bags come out the wrong brown.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the office smells of coffee and the roastery is just downstairs, I can walk down and taste things. What gets to me is the spreadsheets, our sales director wants every promotion tracked in about six tabs, and I'm not quick with that. I've never used any AI tool, people keep telling me to, I just haven't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, good, everyone calm down. At work I'd say it in the kitchen and get back to the autumn promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I like a job where the hardest decision is whether the autumn bag says hazelnut or caramel. If AI just speeds up a few spreadsheets, that's no threat. I've got about nine months saved and my car's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much. I'd keep doing the job, maybe ask a colleague to show me the spreadsheet shortcuts. Keep saving a bit each month like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you build up nine months of savings at 27?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lived with my parents until I was 25 and paid them a small rent. Inês, my girlfriend, thinks I'm too careful with money, but it's how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Coffee prices go up and down, so sometimes the promotions get cut, but the cafés always need menu boards.

say: I'd tell everyone to **calm down** and get back to work.
I'd mention it in the **office kitchen**, not online.
think: I think faster **spreadsheets** are no threat to my job.
I'd feel safe with **nine months saved** and a paid-off car.
do: Keep writing **bag copy** and menu boards as normal.
Ask a colleague for **spreadsheet shortcuts** and keep saving monthly.
S0.quote: I like a job where the hardest decision is whether the autumn bag says hazelnut or caramel.
fieldNote: His **savings** come from careful habits and living at home until 25.
He wants **nothing to change**, and this picture gives him that.
His weak spot is **spreadsheets**, not writing.

steps.text: Keep writing bag copy and café menu boards as usual
Keep putting a fixed sum into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one I don't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably overhyped but we'll see. I don't really post online, so mostly I'd say it to Inês and my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, writing and planning is my whole job. I've never opened an AI tool at work, and I'm not sure I'd know what to type if my manager made me. If they shrink the marketing team, it's the junior who can't use the tools who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company actually does, I don't like jumping first. I'd save more, maybe an extra two hundred a month. If they started cutting people, then I'd look around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I suppose. A low hum of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. What would make you stop waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they didn't replace Clara when she goes on maternity leave next year. That would tell me the tools are doing her work, and mine would be next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about just trying the tools, to be safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it. Every time, I open it, look at the empty box, and close it again. It's silly, I know.

say: I'd say it's probably **overhyped**, but we'll see.
I'd say it **privately** to my girlfriend and brother, not online.
think: I think my **whole job** is the writing and planning on the card.
I'd expect the junior who **can't use the tools** to go first.
do: **Wait and see** what the company does before acting.
Save an **extra two hundred** a month and look around if cuts start.
S1.quote: I've never opened an AI tool at work, and I'm not sure I'd know what to type if my manager made me.
fieldNote: He knows he's **exposed** but still chooses to wait.
He's set a clear **signal**: whether his colleague Clara is replaced.
His public line is **dismissive**, his private view is worried.

steps.text: Watch whether the company replaces Clara during her maternity leave
Save an extra two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's not long at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and the government needs to sort out some support, fast. I'm not political, but that's just obvious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's gone. Funny thing is, the guys roasting the beans downstairs would get three more years than me, just because they use their hands. I've spent four years learning to write about coffee and none learning to make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the head roaster, Bruno, if I could move downstairs and learn roasting, even on less pay. I'd cut the car and sell it, that's eight thousand. I'd also talk to my parents about moving back in for a while if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving downstairs actually be a step down for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay-wise, yes, maybe twenty percent less. Pride-wise, not really. I'd rather be useful with a scoop than useless with a laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Inês say about moving back in with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say no. She's a pharmacist and her job's more secure, so she'd say move in with her properly. That's a bigger conversation than AI.

say: I'd say the **government** must sort out support fast.
I'd insist I'm **not political**, just stating the obvious.
think: I think my **job's gone**, while hands-on roasters get three more years.
I'd regret learning to **write about coffee** but not make it.
do: Ask to move **downstairs** and learn roasting, even for less pay.
Sell the car for about **eight thousand** and consider moving in.
S2.quote: Funny thing is, the guys roasting the beans downstairs would get three more years than me, just because they use their hands.
fieldNote: He immediately spots the **thinking first, robots later** gap inside his own company.
His instinct is to move toward **hands-on** work, not new tools.
His girlfriend's **secure job** shapes the household plan.

steps.text: Ask the head roaster for a trainee roasting job downstairs
Sell the car for about eight thousand
Move in with his girlfriend or parents to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's harder to read, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be sensible about it. I'd probably say that a lot, to be honest, because it lets me not do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the worst amount of time for someone like me, because it's long enough to put off deciding. I'd lose the marketing job around 2031, and I'd probably still be telling myself I had time in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say I'd start learning roasting on Saturdays straight away. Realistically, I'd save harder, maybe four hundred a month, and wait two years to see. Then I'd ask Bruno about moving downstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, in a slow way. Like a bill you keep not opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're quite honest about putting it off. What would help you not do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date. If my manager said, your role ends in March 2030, I'd act. Without a date, I drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Inês, does her timing change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her job's safer, but pharmacies use a lot of software too. If both of us are worried at the same time, I don't know what we'd do.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so let's be sensible.
I'd admit that line lets me **put off** acting.
think: I think five years tempts me to **delay deciding**.
I'd lose the job around **2031** and still feel I had time in 2030.
do: Save about **four hundred** a month and wait two years.
Then ask to move **downstairs** to the roastery.
feel: **Alarmed** slowly, like a bill I keep not opening.
S3.quote: Five years is the worst amount of time for someone like me, because it's long enough to put off deciding.
fieldNote: He's unusually **self-aware** about his habit of drifting.
He says a **firm date** from his manager would make him act.
The risk to his girlfriend's **pharmacy job** adds to his worry.

steps.text: Save about four hundred a month
Wait two years before deciding anything
Ask to move down to the roastery around 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That sounds more like normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, there's time, let's not panic. At work I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years and I'd probably end up roasting coffee instead of writing about it, which my grandfather would find hilarious. He picked coffee on a farm as a boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the marketing job for five or six years. In the meantime I'd do the roasting course the company offers staff, it's one Saturday a month. Around 2032 I'd move downstairs for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. More like a long to-do list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still anxious, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know myself. I'll leave it late. And robots for the roasting come around 2039, so even that's not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone starting in marketing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands as well. I didn't, and every one of these pictures shows me why.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so let's not panic.
I'd say it at work and **actually mean** it, because a decade feels like normal life.
think: I think I'd end up **roasting coffee** instead of writing about it.
I'd still expect the **marketing job** to go within the decade.
do: Keep the marketing job for **five or six** years.
Do the company's monthly **roasting course** and move downstairs around 2032.
feel: **Anxious**, but more like a long to-do list.
S4.quote: Ten years and I'd probably end up roasting coffee instead of writing about it, which my grandfather would find hilarious.
fieldNote: His plan points to **hands-on** coffee work, linked to his grandfather's past.
He stays anxious because he expects to **leave it late**.
He notices robots reach **roasting** by 2039 too.

steps.text: Keep the marketing job for five or six more years
Take the company's Saturday roasting course once a month
Move to the roastery floor around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2031, oddly, more than the fast one, because I'd waste the time. What would help is someone giving me a firm date and a proper training place, not just a website with courses. I'm not against AI, I'm just slow with new things, and every one of these pictures punishes slow people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people downstairs. Everyone talks about office jobs, but the roasters and packers will need to know what's coming too, just later.

headlineQuote: I'm not against AI, I'm just slow with new things, and every one of these pictures punishes slow people.
portrait: Rafael is a 27-year-old **junior marketing executive** at a coffee roaster who has never used AI.
He has **nine months saved** from living at home, and his girlfriend Inês is a pharmacist.
He wants things to stay the same and admits he tends to **drift** rather than decide.
In the AGI pictures he aims to move **downstairs** to hands-on roasting.
He sounds calm in public but turns **alarmed** in private once AGI arrives within five years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2031**, because five years tempts him to **waste** the time.
whatWouldHelp: A **firm date** for his role ending and a real **training place**.
